rows.question: s1-q05-tail
rows.finalText:
The only cache-free point identified was the degenerate "floor" case — **when the whole prefix is already cache-stable because every branch is kept**.

Concretely, in the v6 selector work (implementation phase 4, node `n_1FJ2VN7BZMD0C22JVNB4NGNNPW`), the team added a passing unit test named:

> "token-level selection is viable when the whole prefix is cache-stable — mergeKeepSets returns undefined (floor property)"

The mechanism: `mergeKeepSets` enforces monotone membership (once kept, always kept, so the cached Zone B prefix survives every turn). When all branches are already in the keep-set, it returns `undefined` — a no-op. That no-op floor is the single point where token-level selection touches the context without churning the cache, because it changes nothing.

This is exactly why it was a dead end: under the monotone lock-in constraint, that's the *only* state selection can occupy, so cache-safe token-level selection "provably never fires" — recorded as FM-8 in the final synthesis, one of the two poles of evidence (alongside FM-5, where eviction destroyed load-bearing context) used to retire the DSA-on-branches selector line (v2–v6) entirely.

rows.question: s1-q05-tail
rows.finalText:
The team identified only **one cache-free point** where token-level selection is viable: **the summarizer's compaction step**.

As recorded in the diagnosis phase, every other candidate site for token-level selection (per-turn eviction, Zone C rewrites) sits behind a cache breakpoint, where the cost of invalidating the cached prefix outweighs any benefit the selection could provide. The summarizer's compaction step, by contrast, doesn't disturb a cached prefix — so it's the sole location where selection can operate at token granularity without paying a cache-invalidation penalty.
